query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, tailoring the composition to include an Al-rich reservoir phase enables a sustained, slow diffusion of aluminum to the surface, which promotes the in situ formation of a continuous and coherent Al2O3 protective scale that resists cracking and spalling at temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative atmospheres.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state with a conventional (lower) Al content.
generation.intervention: Increase the Al concentration to create a distinct Al-rich reservoir phase within the alloy microstructure.
generation.conditions: Exposure to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures exceeding 900 °C for prolonged periods.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an Al-rich reservoir phase which feeds Al by slow diffusion to sustain the growth of an adherent Al2O3 layer at the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: A controlled, continuous supply of aluminum from the Al-rich reservoir diffuses to the surface during high-temperature exposure, enabling the formation of a dense and coherent alumina (Al2O3) scale that maintains adhesion and resists spallation by mitigating stress and crack formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with the enhanced Al-rich reservoir will form a slow-growing, continuous, and mechanically robust Al2O3 scale that remains intact under high-temperature oxidative conditions, unlike alloys with standard Al levels which are more prone to oxide cracking and spallation.
generation.baseline: The oxidation behavior of CrFeCoNiX alloys with standard (lower) Al-content, which likely form less coherent and unstable oxide scales that crack or spall under similar conditions.
generation.boundary: Tested in high-temperature (above 900 °C) oxidizing or corrosive environments over extended durations; applicable to both single-phase and multiphase solid-solution states as long as the Al-rich reservoir is distinguishable in the microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in oxide stability, the optimal Al concentration for reservoir formation, and potential interactions with other alloying elements remain uncertain and require further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrFeCoNiX alloys: one modified to include an elevated Al-content forming a measurable Al-rich reservoir phase, and a control alloy with standard Al levels. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature (e.g., 950 °C) exposure in an oxidative atmosphere (e.g., air or controlled oxygen partial pressure) for a prolonged duration (e.g., 100 hours).
measurements: Cross-sectional SEM imaging to assess oxide scale continuity and presence of cracks.
EDS mapping to verify the Al concentration gradients and verify the formation of the Al-rich reservoir phase.
XRD analysis to confirm the formation of Al2O3 and other oxides.
Mass gain measurements as a proxy for oxidation kinetics.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified high-Al alloy does not exhibit a significantly more continuous, coherent, and slow-growing Al2O3 scale (with fewer cracks or spallation events) compared to the baseline alloy under identical conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

At temperatures exceeding 500 °C, the oxidation behavior of traditional and complex alloys (e.g., Ni-Cr, Ni-based superalloys, Fe-Cr, CoCrFeNiMn ‘Cantor’ alloy) has been extensively studied in oxygen-rich environments and over extended periods (from days to hundreds of days,). Key contributors to the process include species transport to the oxide/metal junction within the base alloy, movement across the oxide/metal interface, and passage through the oxide layer. For instance, atmospheric oxidation of CoCrFeNiMn-containing alloys results in a layered oxide film, with Cr-rich inner and Mn-rich outer oxides attributed to outward cation diffusion. In a study by Kim et al., the high-temperature oxidation of FeCrMnNiCo (900–1100 °C in 20% O2/80% N2 for 24 h) showed the formation of layered Cr2O3 and Mn2O3 oxides at 900 °C. This process led to Ni, Fe, and Co enrichment in the base alloy. At 1000–1100 °C, the outer Mn2O3 layer changed to Mn3O4, forming a (Mn, Cr)3O4 ternary oxide with Ni, Fe, and Co in a solid solution. Aluminium rich TiAl, and the TiAl2 and TiAl3 aluminides can form alumina scales but Al poor TiAl and Ti3Al form titania rich scales and oxidise at much higher rates []. For example, when TiAl with 50 at.% Al was oxidised in air at 950, 1100 and 1200 °C, at the two higher temperatures TiO2 scale formed and there was internal oxidation. Parabolic oxidation kinetics were followed at the low temperature where the oxidation was independent of specimen preparation and fabrication method []. Furthermore, the alloying of TiAl with Nb promoted the formation of continuous alumina scale on TiAl (50 at.% Al) at 950 °C independent of surface preparation or exposure environment (air or O2) but the alloying with Hf had a minimal effect []. For Al poor TiAl it is known that the addition of 4 to 12 at.% Nb in Ti–48Al increased oxidation resistance at 850 °C and that the alloys developed continuous bands of dense alumina beneath titania rich surface layer that formed during the early stages of oxidation []. The cross-section image in Figure 9c shows that the scale was composed of two parts (layers), the outer part (bright grey contrast) was (Al,Cr)NbO4 mixed with Al2O3 particles (dark grey contrast) and Hf-rich oxide particles, and the inner part consisted of Al2O3. The Al2O3 layer beneath the outer part was adherent and formed continuously all over the substrate. The scale had lumps over phase boundaries and the inner Al2O3 layer was able to withstand the stresses (without buckling) that resulted from the oxidation of the eutectic. Hf-rich oxide particles were also observed in the oxidized Laves phase.

Internal oxidation had occurred in all facets of the cubic specimen and was deeper along the phase boundaries (Figure 8). reading.lever: Tailor the CrFeCoNiX composition to create an Al-rich reservoir phase that slowly feeds continuous, coherent Al2O3 formation.
reading.why: This approach, inspired by Ti–Al systems with Nb/Si additions, directly addresses oxide cracking by ensuring a controlled, sustained supply of the passivating element.
